title: Lav 3
hookLine: the third round: longing for the Lord, and detachment within (Suhi M4, ang 774)

cards: There's a kind of missing that happens even when someone is already yours. Two people in the same house, and one still looks up when the other walks in. A work trip, and the hotel bed feels too wide.
It isn't loneliness exactly. It's longing that lives right next to love, and keeps it awake. Punjabi folk songs know it well: the bride waiting at the window, the lover across the river.
The third round of the Sikh wedding points that feeling somewhere surprising.

teach.h: ROUND THREE: LONGING FOR THE LORD.
teach.b: The third stanza of the laavan, on Ang seven seventy-four, says, in paraphrase: in the third round, the mind fills with a longing for the Lord, and becomes detached.
Meeting the holy company, by good fortune, one finds the Lord. One speaks the unspoken word, sings the Lord's praises, and the heart is lit with love. The key word is bairaag.
It's usually translated detachment, and that sounds cold.
But in this stanza bairaag is warm: the ache of separation, the yearning of someone who has glimpsed the Beloved and can't settle for less.
The stanza says the mind becomes chaao, eager, and bairaagee, longing, in the same breath. So the detachment here isn't pulling away from the person beside you.
It's that nothing small can be the center anymore: not status, not the guest list, not who was right last week. Longing for God loosens the grip of all of that.
And notice where the longing is found: in the sangat, the holy company. Round three isn't walked alone.
At a Sikh wedding the whole congregation is there, singing; and from the first round, a couple is surrounded by people who share what they care about.
For the soul's journey, round three is the turn from discipline to desire. Round one was duty. Round two washed away fear and ego.
In the soul's reading, round three is when the soul starts to want God, the way someone wants a person they love.

how: At the Anand Karaj, the third of the four laavan is read and sung while the couple walks a third time around the Guru Granth Sahib, with the congregation joining the singing.

o: cold distance from the people you love
a sad song of a bride left alone
a warm longing for the Lord

games.q: the third round — tap the pairs.

s: bairaag in the third lav means pulling away from your spouse
it's longing for God, which loosens the grip of small things.
the third stanza says the Lord is found in the holy company
meeting the sangat, by good fortune, one finds the Lord.

games.q: you've walked two rounds. the third stanza says the mind becomes something. what?
games.why: chaao and bairaagee: eager and longing in the same breath, the mind turned toward the Lord.

practice: Walk a third slow clockwise round, or trace one with your hand, and let yourself feel something you long for, not a thing to buy, but something deeper: peace, closeness, a sense of home.
Don't fix it or explain it; let the longing be there, warm, as you finish. If you pray, say Waheguru, and let the longing be the prayer.

wordCard.voice: Bairaag, longing, detachment, the warm ache for God: in the third round of the Sikh wedding, the mind grows eager and longing, found in the holy company, lit with love for the Lord.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: longing, detachment; in the third lav, the warm ache for God.

carryVoice: Your line: round three: longing. Missing someone can point to what you most deeply want. One round left.

sources.ref: Suhi Mahalla 4, Chhant (the laavan), third stanza, Ang 774
